unit.text:
4 Incremental Indexing
Our approach builds the index incrementally. Instead of rebuilding the full inverted index after every update, new documents are written to a small in-memory segment that is merged into the main index once it exceeds a size threshold. This keeps write latency low while bounding the number of segments a query must scan.
In our experiments the merge threshold of 64 MB gave the best balance between write throughput and query latency (see Table 2).

items.title: Buffer new documents in a small segment and merge later
items.summary: Rather than rebuilding the whole index on each change, new documents go into a small memory-resident segment that is folded into the main index only once it grows past a limit.
items.details:
- Writes stay fast because they touch only the small segment.
- Queries stay fast because the merge step caps how many segments a search must read.
- The size limit is the single tuning point between these two goals.
items.anchor_quote: new documents are written to a small in-memory segment

items.title: A 64 MB merge threshold balanced writes and queries best
items.summary: Among the thresholds the authors tried, merging at 64 MB gave the best trade-off between how fast documents can be written and how fast queries run.
items.details: The supporting measurements are reported in a separate table of the paper.
